name: Health & Wellness
tagline: Symptoms, diseases, vet care, and when to worry — a practical health reference.

entries.q: How often should I take my cat to the vet?
entries.a: Healthy adult cats: once a year for a wellness exam. Kittens need a series of visits every 3–4 weeks until about 16 weeks old for vaccines. Seniors (11+) benefit from twice-yearly exams with bloodwork, since age-related diseases like kidney disease and hyperthyroidism develop quickly. Indoor-only cats still need annual checkups — cats hide illness extremely well.

entries.q: What vaccines do cats need?
entries.a: Core vaccines for all cats: FVRCP (feline viral rhinotracheitis, calicivirus, panleukopenia) and rabies (often legally required). FeLV (feline leukemia) is recommended for all kittens and for adult cats that go outdoors or live with FeLV-positive cats. Kittens start vaccines around 6–8 weeks with boosters every 3–4 weeks until 16+ weeks; adults need periodic boosters per your vet's schedule.

entries.q: My cat is vomiting — when should I worry?
entries.a: An occasional hairball or single vomit with normal behavior afterward is usually fine. See a vet if vomiting happens more than once or twice a month, occurs repeatedly in a day, contains blood or looks like coffee grounds, or comes with lethargy, appetite loss, diarrhea, or weight loss. Repeated unproductive retching or a cat who can't keep water down is an emergency. Chronic vomiting is never "just normal for cats."

entries.q: Are hairballs normal?
entries.a: The occasional hairball (once or twice a month) is common, especially in long-haired cats, but frequent hairballs are not normal — they can indicate overgrooming, skin disease, or gastrointestinal motility problems. Regular brushing, hairball-control diets, and fiber supplements help. A cat retching repeatedly without producing anything needs a vet promptly, as it can mimic asthma or an obstruction.

entries.q: Why is my cat sneezing?
entries.a: Occasional sneezing is normal (dust, perfume, litter). Frequent sneezing usually means an upper respiratory infection — most often herpesvirus or calicivirus — especially with watery eyes and nasal discharge. Other causes: allergies, dental root infections, foreign material in the nose, or (rarely) nasal polyps and tumors. See a vet if sneezing persists more than a few days, discharge turns yellow/green or bloody, or the cat stops eating.

entries.q: Can cats catch colds?
entries.a: Cats get "colds" — upper respiratory infections caused mainly by feline herpesvirus and calicivirus, which spread between cats (not from human colds). Symptoms: sneezing, runny eyes and nose, congestion, mild fever. Most resolve in 7–10 days with rest, hydration, and encouraging eating (warm, smelly food helps a congested cat). See a vet for colored discharge, not eating, lethargy, or breathing difficulty. Note: cats can catch some human flu strains and COVID-19, usually mildly.

entries.q: How do I know if my cat has fleas, and how do I treat them?
entries.a: Signs: intense scratching, overgrooming (especially the lower back and tail base), scabs, and "flea dirt" — black specks in the coat that turn rusty-red on a wet paper towel. Treat every pet in the home with a vet-recommended product (spot-on, oral, or collar) for at least 3 months, and vacuum and wash bedding to clear eggs from the environment. Never use dog flea products on cats — permethrin is highly toxic to them.

entries.q: Do indoor cats need flea and worm prevention?
entries.a: Yes, though risk is lower. Fleas hitchhike in on shoes, clothing, and other pets; mosquitoes (heartworm vectors) get indoors; and cats that hunt house mice or eat fleas can get tapeworms. Many vets recommend year-round prevention for all cats, or at minimum regular checks and fecal testing. Discuss your cat's specific risk with your vet.

entries.q: How do I know if my cat has worms?
entries.a: Signs include rice-like tapeworm segments around the anus or in bedding, spaghetti-like roundworms in vomit or stool, a pot-bellied appearance (especially kittens), diarrhea, weight loss despite good appetite, and a dull coat. Many infected cats show no signs at all, which is why routine fecal exams and deworming matter. Most worms are easily treated with vet-prescribed dewormers; over-the-counter products vary in effectiveness.

entries.q: Do cats need dental care?
entries.a: Absolutely — most cats over age three have some dental disease. Untreated tartar leads to painful gingivitis, tooth resorption, and infections that can affect the heart and kidneys. Gold standard: daily brushing with cat-specific toothpaste (never human toothpaste). Helpful additions: dental diets, VOHC-approved treats, and water additives. Most cats eventually need professional cleanings under anesthesia.

entries.q: Why does my cat have bad breath?
entries.a: Mild fishy breath after eating is normal, but persistent foul breath usually means dental disease — plaque, gingivitis, infected teeth, or painful tooth resorption. Sweet or acetone-like breath can indicate diabetes; ammonia-like breath suggests kidney disease. Bad breath plus drooling, dropping food, or pawing at the mouth warrants a prompt dental exam.

entries.q: What is cat acne and how do I treat it?
entries.a: Feline chin acne appears as blackheads, crusty bumps, or swelling on the chin and lips, caused by overactive sebaceous glands, sometimes aggravated by plastic food bowls (which harbor bacteria). Mild cases: switch to stainless steel or ceramic bowls washed daily, and gently clean the chin with vet-approved antiseptic wipes. Severe, inflamed cases need veterinary treatment with medicated cleansers or antibiotics. Don't squeeze the bumps.

entries.q: How do I tell if my cat is overweight, and how do I help it slim down?
entries.a: You should feel ribs easily under a thin fat layer and see a waist from above and a belly tuck from the side. No palpable ribs, no waist, and a swinging belly pouch suggest excess weight (note: a small primordial pouch is normal). To slim down: measured meals instead of free-feeding, a vet-calculated calorie target, more play, and slow weight loss only — crash dieting can trigger fatal hepatic lipidosis. Aim for 1–2% body weight loss per week under vet guidance.

entries.q: Why is my cat losing weight?
entries.a: Unintentional weight loss — especially with a normal or increased appetite — is a red flag in cats. Common causes: hyperthyroidism, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, intestinal disease (IBD or lymphoma), dental pain, and parasites. Senior cats losing muscle along the spine deserve special attention. Any noticeable weight loss warrants a vet exam with bloodwork; early diagnosis dramatically improves outcomes.

entries.q: Why is my cat drinking so much water?
entries.a: Increased thirst (polydipsia) is one of the most important symptoms in feline medicine. The big three causes are chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, and hyperthyroidism — all common in middle-aged and senior cats, and all far more manageable when caught early. Also possible: urinary tract infection, liver disease, or simply a switch from wet to dry food. Noticeably increased drinking or urination justifies a vet visit with blood and urine tests.

entries.q: What are the signs of kidney disease in cats?
entries.a: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects a large share of senior cats. Early signs: increased thirst and urination, weight loss, and reduced appetite. Later: vomiting, bad breath (ammonia odor), dehydration, dull coat, and lethargy. CKD is diagnosed with blood tests (creatinine, SDMA) and urinalysis. It's not curable but is very manageable — kidney diets, hydration support, and medications can give cats years of good quality life, especially when caught early.

entries.q: What are the signs of diabetes in cats?
entries.a: Classic signs: drinking and urinating much more than usual, ravenous appetite with weight loss, lethargy, and sometimes walking flat on the hocks (diabetic neuropathy). Overweight, middle-aged, male, and indoor cats are at higher risk. Treatment combines insulin (or newer oral medications) with a low-carbohydrate, high-protein diet — and with early aggressive treatment, some cats go into remission.

entries.q: What is hyperthyroidism in cats?
entries.a: Hyperthyroidism — an overactive thyroid gland — is the most common hormonal disease of senior cats. Signs: weight loss despite a huge appetite, hyperactivity, yowling (especially at night), vomiting, racing heart, and an unkempt coat. Diagnosed with a simple blood test (T4). Treatment options include daily medication (methimazole), radioactive iodine (often curative), prescription diet, or surgery. Untreated, it damages the heart and kidneys.

entries.q: What are FIV and FeLV?
entries.a: FIV (feline immunodeficiency virus) spreads mainly through deep bite wounds; infected cats often live near-normal lifespans with good care and can safely live with non-fighting housemates. FeLV (feline leukemia virus) spreads through prolonged close contact (grooming, shared bowls) and is more serious, suppressing immunity and causing cancers. Both are diagnosed with a quick blood test. Neither infects humans or dogs. Keep positive cats indoors, healthy, and stress-free.

entries.q: What is FIP (feline infectious peritonitis)?
entries.a: FIP is caused by a mutation of the common, usually harmless feline coronavirus. It mainly strikes cats under two, causing fever that doesn't respond to antibiotics, lethargy, weight loss, and either fluid in the belly/chest ("wet" form) or neurological/eye signs ("dry" form). Once uniformly fatal, FIP is now highly treatable with antiviral drugs (GS-441524/remdesivir-class), with cure rates above 80% in many studies. Seek a vet experienced with FIP treatment immediately.

entries.q: My male cat is straining to pee — is this an emergency?
entries.a: YES. A male cat going in and out of the litter box producing little or no urine may have a urethral obstruction, which is fatal within 24–48 hours without treatment. Signs: straining, crying in the box, licking the genitals, vomiting, hiding, and a painful belly. This is one of the true drop-everything cat emergencies — go to a vet or emergency clinic immediately, even at night.

entries.q: How do I know if my cat has a urinary tract infection?
entries.a: Signs of urinary trouble: frequent trips to the box with small amounts of urine, straining, blood-tinged urine, crying while urinating, peeing outside the box, and excessive genital licking. In young cats it's usually feline idiopathic cystitis (stress-related bladder inflammation) rather than bacterial infection; true UTIs are more common in older cats. All need a vet — urinalysis distinguishes the causes, and males with these signs can progress to a life-threatening blockage.

entries.q: My cat is constipated — what should I do?
entries.a: Signs: straining in the box with little result, small hard dry stools, decreased appetite, or vomiting. Mild cases may respond to increased water (wet food, fountains), a teaspoon of plain canned pumpkin, and vet-approved laxatives like lactulose. Never give human laxatives or enemas — some are deadly to cats. No stool for 2–3 days, repeated straining, or lethargy needs a vet; chronic constipation can become megacolon. Note: straining can also mean a urinary blockage, which is an emergency.

entries.q: My cat has diarrhea — when does it need a vet?
entries.a: A single soft stool in an otherwise normal cat can be watched for 24–48 hours with plenty of water available. See a vet sooner for: diarrhea lasting more than two days, blood or black tarry stool, vomiting alongside, lethargy, kittens or seniors (they dehydrate fast), or known toxin exposure. Common causes range from diet changes and parasites to IBD, infections, and hyperthyroidism. Bring a stool sample to the appointment.

entries.q: How can I tell if my cat is in pain?
entries.a: Cats hide pain instinctively. Subtle signs: hiding, decreased grooming (or overgrooming one spot), reluctance to jump, sleeping more, hunched posture, squinted eyes, flattened ears, reduced appetite, litter box avoidance, purring at odd times, and uncharacteristic aggression when touched. The "feline grimace scale" (ear position, eye squinting, muzzle tension) is a validated tool vets use. Any persistent behavior change deserves a pain-focused vet exam.

entries.q: Why is my cat limping?
entries.a: Common causes: soft-tissue sprains from jumps, bite wounds or abscesses (very common in outdoor cats), torn claws, foreign objects in the paw, arthritis in older cats, and fractures. Check the paw for swelling, wounds, and claw damage. A mild limp with normal behavior can be rested and monitored for 24–48 hours; see a vet for non-weight-bearing lameness, swelling, fever, or a limp lasting more than two days. Never give human painkillers — ibuprofen and acetaminophen are toxic to cats.

entries.q: Why does my cat have eye discharge or watery eyes?
entries.a: A little dark crust in the corners is normal. Persistent watery eyes suggest herpesvirus flare-ups, allergies, or blocked tear ducts (common in flat-faced breeds). Yellow-green discharge, squinting, redness, or pawing at the eye indicates infection, a corneal ulcer, or injury — eye problems can deteriorate fast, so these warrant a vet within a day. Wipe gently with a damp cotton pad, and never use human eye drops without veterinary direction.

entries.q: How do I know if my cat has ear mites?
entries.a: Ear mites cause intense itching, head shaking, ear scratching, and a distinctive dark, crumbly discharge resembling coffee grounds. They're highly contagious between pets (common in kittens) but don't infest humans. A vet confirms with a microscope — important because yeast and bacterial infections look similar but need different treatment. Modern single-dose spot-on treatments are very effective; treat all pets in the household.

entries.q: What does ringworm look like in cats?
entries.a: Ringworm is a fungal skin infection (not a worm) causing circular patches of hair loss with scaly, crusty skin, often on the face, ears, and paws — though some cats carry it with no visible signs. It's contagious to humans and other pets, so handle with care and wash hands. Diagnosis: fungal culture, PCR, or Wood's lamp screening. Treatment combines oral antifungals, medicated dips/shampoos, and environmental cleaning for several weeks.

entries.q: Can cats have allergies?
entries.a: Yes — cats commonly suffer from flea allergy (most common; one bite can trigger weeks of itching), environmental allergies/atopy (pollen, dust mites), and food allergies (usually to a protein like chicken or beef, not grain). Signs: itching, overgrooming, bald patches, scabby "miliary" dermatitis, recurrent ear infections, and sometimes sneezing or asthma-like signs. Diagnosis is stepwise: rigorous flea control first, then a vet-supervised elimination diet, then allergy testing.

entries.q: Why is my cat coughing? Could it be asthma?
entries.a: A coughing cat — crouched low, neck extended, with repeated hacking — is often mistaken for hairball retching, but coughing without producing a hairball suggests feline asthma, especially in young to middle-aged cats. Other causes: heartworm, lungworm, pneumonia, and heart disease. Asthma is managed well with inhaled or oral corticosteroids and bronchodilators. Open-mouth breathing, blue gums, or rapid breathing at rest (over ~40 breaths/min sleeping) is an emergency.

entries.q: Why is my cat's third eyelid showing?
entries.a: The third eyelid (nictitating membrane) is the whitish film at the inner corner of the eye. Briefly visible when sleepy is normal, but persistent protrusion — especially in both eyes — signals illness: dehydration, GI disease, fever, eye injury, or neurological issues like Horner's syndrome. One or both third eyelids showing for more than a day, or with other symptoms, needs a vet exam.

entries.q: What symptoms mean my cat needs an emergency vet right now?
entries.a: Go immediately for: open-mouth or labored breathing; male cat straining to urinate; suspected poisoning (lilies, antifreeze, medications); collapse or inability to walk; seizures; severe trauma (hit by car, falls); sudden hind-leg paralysis with crying (aortic thromboembolism); repeated vomiting with lethargy; not eating for 48+ hours; pale or blue gums; eye injuries; and difficulty giving birth. When unsure, call an emergency clinic — describing symptoms by phone is free.

entries.q: My cat won't eat — how long is too long?
entries.a: Cats should never go more than 24–48 hours without food. Unlike dogs, fasting cats can develop hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver), a life-threatening condition — and overweight cats are at highest risk. Try warming food, strong-smelling options (tuna juice, churu-style treats), and stress reduction, but if a cat refuses food for more than a day or shows other symptoms, see a vet promptly. Appetite loss is the single most common early sign of feline illness.

entries.q: Is pet insurance worth it for cats?
entries.a: It depends on your finances. Emergency surgery (urinary blockage, foreign body) commonly runs $2,000–$6,000+, and chronic diseases cost hundreds yearly. Insurance makes the most sense when started young, before pre-existing conditions are excluded. Alternatives: a dedicated savings account funded monthly. Compare deductibles, reimbursement rates, annual caps, and exclusions — and note most plans exclude dental cleanings and pre-existing conditions.

entries.q: Why is my cat's coat greasy or unkempt?
entries.a: A healthy cat keeps itself immaculate, so a greasy, clumped, or dandruffy coat is a health signal, not a grooming failure. Common causes: obesity (can't reach to groom), arthritis pain, dental pain (grooming hurts), hyperthyroidism, kidney disease, and skin conditions. Senior cats with sudden coat changes especially need a checkup. Address the underlying cause — then help with gentle brushing.

entries.q: Why does my cat drool?
entries.a: Some cats drool when blissfully relaxed and kneading — that's harmless "happy drool." Sudden or excessive drooling, however, suggests dental disease, mouth ulcers, nausea, a foreign object in the mouth, kidney disease, or toxin exposure (including licking topical products or bitter medications). Drooling with pawing at the mouth, bad breath, or appetite loss needs a vet exam.

entries.q: Why does my cat keep shaking its head?
entries.a: Persistent head shaking usually means ear trouble: ear mites, yeast or bacterial infections, polyps, or foreign material. Check for redness, odor, and discharge. Repeated shaking and scratching can burst blood vessels in the ear flap, creating a painful aural hematoma that needs treatment. Ears that look dirty or smell bad warrant a vet visit rather than home cleaning, since a ruptured eardrum changes what's safe to use.
